passage: I sit between Charu and Vandana in the accounts office, so I saw the whole thing. Around eleven, a formula error of Vandana's turned the team's shared sheet into a mess of red cells, and she went pink, fixing it fast. A few minutes later Charu, staring at her own screen, let out a low, satisfied chortle, shoulders shaking, hand over her mouth. Vandana's head snapped up. She looked at Charu, then at the sheet, and her jaw tightened. I couldn't tell what Charu was laughing at. It could have been a message, a video, or relief at finishing her report. It could have been the red cells. At lunch Vandana asked quietly, "Was that about my mistake?" Charu looked horrified. "No! My sister sent a photo of her cat stuck in a cooking pot." She showed it. Vandana laughed too, but I noticed she kept a little distance for the rest of the afternoon.

qa.q: What photo had Charu's sister sent?
qa.a: A photo of her cat stuck in a cooking pot.

qa.q: What was Vandana feeling when Charu chortled?
qa.a: Vandana likely felt embarrassed and hurt, suspecting the laugh was mocking her mistake, though it could have been amusement at something else, which it was.

qa.q: What was wise about Vandana's question at lunch?
qa.a: She asked quietly and privately instead of assuming, which gave Charu the chance to explain.

qa.q: How might Charu have felt when Vandana asked?
qa.a: Charu was horrified, and probably sorry, that her private laugh had seemed aimed at a colleague's error.

grounding: It illustrates how a quiet chortle can be private amusement, yet feel mocking when it comes just after someone's mistake, so context decides the reading.

passage: Between customers at her family's sweet shop in Sangli, Seema checked her phone. Nikita had written: "failed the driving test AGAIN. inspector said I nearly reversed into the temple wall." Seema grinned at the picture in her head and typed, "lol 😂 same as my first try." Then she paused. Nikita's messages were usually full of emojis; this one had none. Seema looked at her own lol. To her it meant, I'm with you, it happens. To Nikita it might look like laughing at her. She added: "sorry, that lol was meant as a hug. you okay?" A minute later: "honestly no. Aai's upset about the fees." Seema set the phone beside the jalebi tray and wrote slowly, "want to come by after six? I'll save you the warm ones." Nikita sent back "haha ok 🙂". Seema couldn't tell if the haha was real, but the smile looked like a yes.

qa.q: What did Nikita nearly reverse into?
qa.a: The temple wall.

qa.q: Why did Seema add a second message after her lol?
qa.a: Seema felt uneasy that Nikita, who usually used emojis, might read the lol as mockery, when Seema meant it as sympathy.

qa.q: What can friends do when a lol might be misread?
qa.a: Add plain words, as Seema did with "that lol was meant as a hug", and ask how the person really is.

qa.q: How might Nikita have read Seema's first reply?
qa.a: Already upset about failing and about Aai's worry, Nikita might have felt laughed at rather than supported.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult using lol and laughing emoji to soften a message, then seeing that the same lol can read as humour, politeness or mockery.

subtype: Types of laughter and social bonding [Expressing]
passage:
Faculty adviser's note, Thursday film club.
Irfan has a laugh you can hear from the corridor. Tonight, during the comedy screening, his big belly laugh at the goat scene set off the whole room; even the shy first-years were wiping their eyes. Elizabeth, our exchange student from Leeds, jumped the first time he guffawed and glanced at me, eyebrows raised. She told me afterwards that back home a laugh that loud in a public room might seem a bit much. By the second half she was chuckling along, and at the end she and Irfan were doing the goat's bleat together at the door. When a first-year said the loud laughs made the dialogue hard to hear, Irfan dropped to a quieter chuckle, and nobody made it awkward. I've asked Irfan to help run next month's screening, because that laugh brings people in. I'll also remind everyone to keep the dialogue audible.

qa.q: Where is Elizabeth from?
qa.a: Leeds.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth first feel about Irfan's guffaw?
qa.a: She was startled and a little unsure, since at home a laugh that loud in public might seem too much; by the end she felt at ease and joined in.

qa.q: What did the adviser plan after the screening?
qa.a: To ask Irfan to help run the next screening, and to remind everyone to keep the dialogue audible.

qa.q: How did the shy first-years experience Irfan's laugh?
qa.a: It set them off laughing too and drew them into the fun, though one of them found it hard to hear the dialogue.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult whose belly laughs and guffaws build shared closeness, while showing that a loud laugh can feel bold to someone from another culture.

passage:
Dear Rukmini akka,
You asked why I sounded strange on the phone on Sunday. I'd been crying, and not for the first time that week. End-semester exams finished on Friday, and instead of feeling free I sat on the hostel stairs and cried for twenty minutes over a lost pen. Then again on Saturday in the shower, and again when Amma asked if I was eating properly. I used to think tears meant I was weak. Now I think my body was letting out a whole semester of tension. Still, it was happening a lot, so on Monday I booked a slot with the college counsellor. She was kind. She said crying after a long strain is common, and asked about my sleep and whether I had someone to talk to. I said I had you. This week I'm sleeping more and walking with Jaya in the evenings.
Call me on Thursday?
Gopika

qa.q: What did Gopika cry over on the hostel stairs?
qa.a: A lost pen.

qa.q: How did Gopika feel about the tears at first, and how does Gopika see them now?
qa.a: At first Gopika felt ashamed, thinking tears meant weakness; now Gopika sees them as a release of a semester's tension, though they came often enough to be worth seeing the counsellor.

qa.q: Which steps is Gopika taking?
qa.a: Seeing the college counsellor, sleeping more, walking with Jaya in the evenings and talking to Rukmini.

qa.q: How might Rukmini have felt hearing Gopika's strange voice on Sunday?
qa.a: Rukmini was probably worried, which is why she asked; the letter likely reassures her that Gopika is getting support 🤍

grounding: It illustrates a young adult crying often after exams, seeing tears as release rather than weakness, and choosing rest, a trusted person and counselling.

passage:
Dear Anjali,
I keep thinking about what you said after your Dada's funeral, that the aunties whispered because you didn't cry. So let me tell you about my convocation on Saturday. When they called my name, I walked up the steps and burst into tears. Proper, messy weeping. Ingrid from my lab rushed over afterwards with tissues: "Oh no, what happened?" Nothing had happened! It was joy, and relief after four years of late nights. Nani, in the second row, was weeping too, for her own reasons; she said later it was for Nana, who didn't live to see it. Same tears, different meanings. And you, dry-eyed at the cremation, were grieving as much as anyone there. People show it differently; your family shows it with rituals and cooking, mine with a lot of noise.
Come over on Sunday? I'll make chai and you can tell me about your Dada.
Rashmi

qa.q: Who was sitting in the second row at the convocation?
qa.a: Nani.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when the tears came on stage?
qa.a: Rashmi felt joy and relief after four years of late nights, not sadness, even though Ingrid read the weeping as distress.

qa.q: What is Rashmi offering Anjali?
qa.a: Reassurance that dry eyes do not mean less grief, and time together on Sunday to talk about Anjali's Dada.

qa.q: What was it like for Anjali when the aunties whispered at the funeral?
qa.a: Anjali likely felt judged and misunderstood while grieving deeply in her own way without tears.

grounding: It illustrates that weeping at a graduation or a funeral can mean joy, relief or grief, that cultures differ in showing it, and that support respects the person's own meaning.

passage:
Hi Parul,
Lesson learnt on Friday, and I'm still slightly pink about it. Rehan's cousin got us passes to a sitar recital at the old auditorium. The final raga built and built until my heart was racing, and when it ended I jumped up and whooped, the way we do at the college fest. Silence. A man in front turned around. Some people were still sitting with their eyes closed, soaking it in; the applause came a few seconds later, soft and long. The sitarist smiled in my direction, so maybe she didn't mind, but I felt like I'd shouted in a temple. Compare that to your graduation last year, when your whole family screamed your name and nobody blinked. Same joy, different room. Next time I'll watch what the audience does first, and save the whoops for the cricket ground and your next big day.
Love,
Salma

qa.q: What instrument was played at the recital?
qa.a: The sitar.

qa.q: How did Salma feel after whooping?
qa.a: Salma felt embarrassed and self-conscious, "still slightly pink", as if shouting in a temple, though the sitarist's smile suggested she may not have minded.

qa.q: What does Salma plan to do next time?
qa.a: Watch what the audience does first, and save the whoops for places like the cricket ground.

qa.q: How might the listeners with closed eyes have felt at the whoop?
qa.a: They were likely jolted out of a quiet moment they were soaking in, even if they understood it came from joy.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult learning that whooping is welcome at a fest or graduation but jarring at a quiet recital, so awareness of the venue is a form of respect.

subtype: Yelling at work or home and de-escalation [Regulating]
passage:
Subject: Yesterday's stand-up, and picking it up again
Hi Vaibhav,
I want to come back to yesterday. When the delivery date slipped and you started shouting across the table, I kept my voice low, said, "Let's pick this up tomorrow when we're both calmer," and left the room. I did that on purpose. I could see you were under pressure from the client, and I do want to solve this with you.
I also need to be clear: I'm not okay with being shouted at. My hands were shaking afterwards. I spoke to Meenal, our team lead, last evening, and she's happy to sit in if either of us wants. If it happens again, I'll step out again.
Can we meet at 3 today in the small room? I've listed three options for a new date below; I think the second is realistic if we split the testing.
Seema

qa.q: What time did Seema suggest meeting?
qa.a: At 3 today in the small room.

qa.q: What was Seema feeling after the shouting?
qa.a: Seema felt shaken, with hands shaking afterwards, yet chose to stay calm and still wanted to solve the problem together.

qa.q: Which parts of Seema's email help to de-escalate?
qa.a: Naming what happened calmly, recognising the client pressure on Vaibhav, setting a clear limit, involving the team lead, and offering a concrete time and options.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav read this email?
qa.a: Vaibhav may feel embarrassed but also relieved that Seema still wants to work it out, while knowing clearly that shouting is not acceptable.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult meeting a colleague's raised voice by staying calm, lowering their own tone, asking to continue later and getting support.

subtype: Sighing to hide or show stress [Regulating]
passage:
Shalini: ugh. I think I upset Harish today
Keerthana: what happened?
Shalini: he asked me to redo the chart for the third time and I let out this huge sigh. like a whole balloon deflating
Shalini: didn't say a word. just the sigh
Keerthana: 😬 from his side that probably sounded like "you're wasting my time"
Shalini: I was just tired!! the sigh wasn't at him
Keerthana: he doesn't know that though
Shalini: true. his face kind of closed after
Keerthana: try the slow kind next time. breathe out long through your nose, no sound, then say "give me ten minutes"
Shalini: the secret sigh 😅
Keerthana: exactly. same calm, no audience
Shalini: okay. messaging him now to say sorry, it was the day, not him
Keerthana: 👍 good call

qa.q: How many times had Harish asked for the chart to be redone?
qa.a: Three times; this was the third.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling when the sigh came out?
qa.a: Shalini was tired and frustrated with the day rather than annoyed at Harish, though from his side it could sound dismissive.

qa.q: What did Keerthana suggest for next time?
qa.a: A silent, slow breath out through the nose followed by words like "give me ten minutes", so the calming works without an audience.

qa.q: How did the sigh probably land with Harish?
qa.a: It likely sounded like "you're wasting my time"; his face closed, so he may have felt dismissed.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult learning that a slow, quiet sigh can steady nerves while a loud sigh at a colleague can feel dismissive.

passage: Leila always whistled on her walk to the bakery in Marseille, a tuneless little song that meant the morning was going well. Her friend Esther said it was like walking beside a kettle. On Saturday, waiting for the tram at Castellane, they heard a different whistle: two sharp notes aimed at Esther from a man leaning on a pillar. Then again, louder, with a "hey, beautiful." Esther pulled her jacket closed and stared hard at the timetable. Leila's own tune died in her throat. Same sound, she thought, but his wasn't a song. It was a hand on the shoulder nobody asked for. "Let's move," Leila said, and they walked to the far end of the platform, near the staff booth. Esther told the attendant what had happened. The attendant nodded, radioed security, and stayed beside them until the tram came. Leila didn't whistle again until they were off the tram.

qa.q: Where did Leila usually whistle?
qa.a: On her walk to the bakery.

qa.q: What was Leila feeling when her own tune died?
qa.a: Leila felt uneasy and angry on Esther's behalf, seeing that the same sound she used for joy had become an unwelcome intrusion.

qa.q: What did they do that helped?
qa.a: They moved away to the staff booth and reported it; the attendant radioed security and stayed with them until the tram came.

qa.q: What was it like for Esther when the man whistled?
qa.a: She likely felt uncomfortable and unsafe, pulling her jacket closed and staring at the timetable to shut out the attention.

grounding: It illustrates that whistling can express calm or joy, but whistling at a person in public can be harassment, and a targeted person may leave and report it.

passage:
Hi Rajni,
Quick one after our call. While I walked through the survey plan, you said "mm-hmm" a lot, which usually tells me you're following. But around the ten-minute mark the mm-hmms went flat and came a bit late, and I could hear typing. I wondered if you were juggling something else, which is completely fine; I just want to be sure the sampling part landed. Then, when I suggested moving the field visits to November, you said "hmm..." and paused. I couldn't tell if that was thinking, doubt or a polite no. Rather than guess, I'd like to ask: are you okay with November, or does it clash with something? And shall I send a two-line summary of the sampling bit?
No rush. Honest answers welcome, including "I was replying to my boss."
Yash

qa.q: What month did Yash suggest for the field visits?
qa.a: November.

qa.q: How did Yash feel after Rajni's "hmm"?
qa.a: Yash felt uncertain whether it meant thinking, doubt or a polite no, and a little worried that the sampling part had not landed.

qa.q: How did Yash handle the uncertainty?
qa.a: By asking directly and kindly about November, offering a short summary, and making an honest answer easy, instead of assuming.

qa.q: How might Rajni feel reading the email?
qa.a: Probably relieved by the gentle tone and the easy chance for Rajni to say if Rajni was distracted or unsure about November.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult hearing mm-hmm as following, a flat mm-hmm as possible distraction and hmm as thinking or doubt, and checking rather than assuming.
